[ORIGINAL USER REQUEST]
[PREVIOUS WORK]
**Executive Summary**

The manufacturer faces a textbook low-end disruption: a new entrant is capturing the mid-market with “good enough” durability sold at roughly 60 cents on the dollar through a channel-avoidance model. Six consecutive quarters of volume decline mean this is no longer a strategic planning exercise; it is a **retail-crisis management problem**. Shelf space is at immediate risk, and engineering culture cannot be “persuaded” into a multi-year platform overhaul with slogans.

The correct response is still **“Fortify and Flank,”** but only if executed with brutal honesty about appliance economics, manufacturing timelines, and organizational power.

- **Fortify the premium line** by converting it into a *system* (product + certified service + TCO guarantee) that the disruptor cannot replicate without building a domestic logistics network. Do not attempt to build a captive white-glove fleet; instead, weaponize the retailer’s existing delivery infrastructure.
- **Flank with an Essential tier** that is **retail-first**, not DTC-first. Large-appliance direct-to-consumer economics are negative once last-mile delivery, installation, haul-away, and returns are fully loaded. The Essential line will instead launch through a club or value-retail partner willing to accept thinner margins in exchange for traffic. It will hit the disruptor’s price band through honest *value engineering*—material substitution, reduced safety-factor overhang, and a 10-year design life—not through the fantasy that a premium chassis can simply be stripped of WiFi and sold at a 35% discount.
- **Restructure the cost base on a 4-year horizon.** A unified modular platform is the right long-term answer, but in the appliance industry, clean-sheet platform development (tooling, UL/CSA certification, supply-chain qualification, plant retooling) requires 36–48 months. The company cannot wait. Essential v1.0 will be a value-engineered derivative of existing architecture, launched within 12 months, while the true modular platform is developed in parallel.

This is not a retreat from premium. It is a refusal to cede the mid-market to an inferior standard—executed with the operational rigor that a six-quarter bleed demands.

---

## 1. Strategic Diagnosis: Why the Entrant Is 40% Cheaper

Before designing a response, diagnose the adversary’s cost structure. The 40% gap is almost certainly driven by structural advantages the incumbent cannot fully replicate, not merely by “being online.”

| Disruptor Advantage | Likely Mechanism | Incumbent Implication |
|---------------------|------------------|----------------------|
| **Offshore manufacturing** | Contract production in lower-cost regions with minimized domestic overhead. | Labor and content costs are 15–25% below the incumbent’s blended cost base. |
| **Channel avoidance** | Pure-play DTC/listings on marketplaces; no retail slotting, co-op advertising, or sales-staff overhead. | The incumbent’s retail cost stack (margin, markdown reserve, logistics to store) is real and unavoidable for its core business. |
| **Minimal service infrastructure** | No field-service network; warranty claims handled by mail-in/component swap or third-party admin. Customer self-installs or uses gig-economy labor. | The disruptor externalizes installation risk and last-mile cost to the consumer. |
| **Shorter design life** | Components (bearings, seals, motors) specified for 5–7 year duty cycles rather than 20. | Lower BOM cost through lighter-gauge materials, smaller motors, and reduced safety-factor overengineering. |
| **Lower warranty reserves** | Aggressive reserves or limited statutory coverage in near-term financials. | A pricing advantage that may prove fragile if failure rates spike, but is real in the market today. |
| **Vertical integration or direct import** | Owns container-level logistics; no distributor tier. | Freight and import cost advantages on finished goods. |

**The implication:** The entrant is not merely “selling online.” It is selling a *different product* through a *different cost architecture*. The incumbent cannot close this gap with channel arbitrage alone. It must match the entrant’s price band with a purpose-built cost structure, while using its 30-year reputation and domestic infrastructure to make the premium tier untouchable.

---

## 2. The Crisis Window: Immediate Stabilization (Months 0–6)

With six quarters of decline, the highest priority is **stopping the retail bleeding** before the Essential line exists. Phase 1 must deliver near-term revenue protection and shelf-space retention, not strategic vision decks.

### 2.1 Retail Bridge Program: Margin Dollars, Not List-Price Cuts
Retail partners are demanding price concessions because their category profit is under pressure. Do not cut list price. Instead, offer a **90-day bridge package** of temporary, reversible trade support:
- **Turn-growth spiffs:** Fund in-store sales associate incentives ($25–$50/unit) on 2–3 hero SKUs to maintain sell-through velocity without changing the price ticket.
- **Display financing:** Offer 100% co-op funding for premium-line brand shops or end-cap resets, conditioned on maintaining full facings for the bridge period.
- **Floor-plan relief:** Extend dating or inventory protection on aging stock to prevent retailers from marking down and creating a reference-price anchor.
- **Category P&L transparency:** Open the books. Show the retailer exactly what the disruptor’s online price implies for in-store service costs, and demonstrate that the incumbent’s premium line delivers higher *margin dollars per square foot* than the low-priced alternative when attach rates (extended warranty, delivery, haul-away) are included.

### 2.2 Contingency for Partial Delisting
If a top retailer accelerates delisting or slashes facings before the Essential tier is ready:
- **Activate alternate channels immediately:** Divert inventory to builder/remodel contractors, property-management bulk channels, and regional appliance dealers who are not aligned with the big-box entrant.
- **Golden-SKU protection:** Negotiate to keep 2–3 hero SKUs in distribution even if the broader range is trimmed. A narrow presence is better than absence.
- **Temporary regional direct program:** In delisted markets only, offer DTC with white-glove delivery—but treat it as a defensive loss-leader, not a scalable channel.

### 2.3 Internal Rapid Response
- **Disruptor teardown:** Buy 50 units. Subject them to accelerated-life testing, BOM analysis, and supplier tracing. Publish findings internally in 60 days. Knowing whether the entrant’s motor is truly under-specified or merely smaller is critical to Essential engineering.
- **SKU Triage:** Halt production of the bottom 20% of SKUs by volume. Free plant capacity and working capital for Essential v1.0 without adding capital expense.

---

## 3. Fortify Premium: Service Moats Through Existing Infrastructure

The original proposal treated white-glove service as a bundling tactic. For a mid-sized OEM without a captive last-mile fleet, this is operationally illiterate. The correct approach is to **orchestrate service through the retailer’s existing delivery network** and third-party risk transfer.

### 3.1 Certified Install Network
Rather than building a proprietary fleet, launch a **“Certified Install”** program:
- The manufacturer trains and audits the retailer’s (or regional third-party) delivery technicians on product-specific installation, connectivity setup, and haul-away.
- The OEM subsidizes a per-unit certification fee ($40–$60) and provides digital dispatch tools.
- Retailers bill consumers directly for installation ($150–$250) but wear the “trusted partner” halo of the OEM’s certification badge.
- **Why it works:** Retailers gain incremental service revenue; the OEM gains a moat the online pure-play cannot match without years of logistics build-out.

### 3.2 Warranty as Financial Product
Launch a 10-year extended warranty and preventative-maintenance plan, but **underwrite it through a third-party insurer** (e.g., Assurant, CNA). The OEM captures a royalty and brand association without carrying the long-tail liability. The disruptor’s 1-year limited warranty is exposed at the point of sale via a TCO calculator: *“Replace twice over 10 years vs. protect once.”*

### 3.3 Retail-Exclusive Configuration
Give brick-and-mortar partners exclusive SKUs—specific finishes, larger capacities, or “pro” trim packages—not available online. This converts the retailer from a price enforcer into a co-investor in premium differentiation. These SKUs carry a 5–8% wholesale premium and are fenced from all DTC/marketplace listings.

---

## 4. Flank with Essential: Honest Cost Engineering and Retail-First Launch

The previous plan proposed a DTC-first Essential line and claimed channel arbitrage would close half the price gap. For large appliances, this is financially false. Below is the honest unit-economic reality.

### 4.1 Why DTC Fails for White Goods
| Cost Element | DTC Estimate (Large Appliance) |
|--------------|-------------------------------|
| **Consumer Price** | $650 |
| **COGS (value-engineered)** | $330 |
| **Last-mile delivery + install** | ($140) |
| **Haul-away / reverse logistics reserve** | ($45) |
| **Customer acquisition (paid search/affiliate)** | ($90) |
| **Returns / damage reserve (≈8%)** | ($52) |
| **Contribution Margin** | **($7)** |

DTC is contribution-negative for a $650 appliance. The “retail margin savings” are consumed entirely by fulfillment complexity. The Essential line will therefore launch **retail-first**, through a club or value-oriented big-box partner willing to accept a 12–18% margin (vs. 30–35% for premium) in exchange for traffic velocity and exclusive market-window rights.

### 4.2 Honest Product Economics: The Essential Tier
| Dimension | Premium Line | Essential Line | Disruptor |
|-----------|--------------|----------------|-----------|
| **Retail Price** | $1,000 | **$650** | $600 |
| **Retailer Margin** | 35% | 15% (club/value model) | N/A (DTC) |
| **Net to OEM** | $650 | **$553** | — |
| **COGS** | $480 | **$330** | ~$250–280 |
| **OEM Gross Margin** | 26% | **40%** | — |
| **Design Life** | 20 years | **10–12 years** | 5–7 years |
| **Warranty** | 10 years | **5 years** | 1 year |
| **Core Motor/Chassis** | Heavy-duty proprietary | *Derivatives* of existing platform, value-engineered | Light-duty commodity |
| **Features** | 12 cycles, WiFi, smart diagnostics, stainless | 4 cycles, mechanical controls, coated steel, clean utility | 4–6 cycles, basic digital, plastic trim |

**How the math works:**
- **Channel efficiency:** Selling through a club/value retailer at 15% margin avoids the DTC logistics trap and still leaves the OEM with healthy gross dollars ($223/unit vs. $170/unit on premium).
- **Honest value engineering:** The Essential line is *not* the premium chassis in disguise. It uses:
  - **Material substitution:** Commercial-grade coated steel and reinforced composites where premium uses heavier-gauge stainless; plastic tubs/drums where engineering validation permits for a 10-year cycle count.
  - **Right-sized motor:** A shared motor *architecture* but with reduced over-engineering (e.g., 1/3 HP vs. 1/2 HP where duty-cycle analysis supports it), not the identical unit.
  - **Control simplification:** Mechanical rotary switches and standard wiring harnesses eliminate touchscreen assemblies, IoT modules, and software-validation costs.
  - **Dimensional standardization:** Fewer unique stampings and a narrower color range reduce tooling and changeover costs.
  - **Reduced warranty duration:** A 5-year warranty aligns with the 10-year design life and cuts reserve costs by roughly half vs. the premium tier.

**Positioning:** *“Built to outlast the category, without the extras you don’t need.”* This is honest democratization, not desperation. The Essential line does not pretend to be the premium product; it promises to beat the disruptor on durability and safety at a similar price.

---

## 5. Platform and Cost Architecture: A Realistic Timeline

The previous plan proposed an 18–24 month modular platform transition. In the appliance industry, this is fiction. The incumbent must separate **short-term survival** from **long-term restructuring**.

### 5.1 Essential v1.0 (Months 6–15): Derivative, Not Clean-Sheet
Do not wait for a unified platform. Task the carve-out engineering team (see Section 7) to:
- Modify existing stampings and assemblies to accept the simplified control and trim packages.
- Qualify lower-cost material suppliers for non-structural components.
- Pilot in one plant with existing equipment.

This is value engineering on a known architecture, not a redesign. It can be executed in 9–12 months because safety-critical systems (gas lines, electrical enclosures) remain proven.

### 5.2 Unified Modular Platform (Years 2–4): The Clean-Sheet Program
Only now launch the true platform unification:
- **Shared core architecture:** A family of motors, pumps, and frames with tier-specific configurations (heavy-gauge housing for premium; lighter-gauge, same architecture, for Essential).
- **Late-stage postponement:** Common base units differentiated by control modules, trim kits, and software in the final assembly cells.
- **Supplier consolidation:** Use the combined 3-year volume forecast to negotiate scale pricing on the shared motor family and stamped components.

**Honest milestones:**
- Month 18: Platform engineering spec freeze.
- Month 30: Tooling completion and UL/CSA submission.
- Month 36: Pilot production and field validation.
- Month 42–48: Full cutover.

---

## 6. Channel Architecture: Protect Retail While Attacking the Mid-Market

| Channel | Role | Product | Terms |
|---------|------|---------|-------|
| **Premium Authorized Retail** | High-touch discovery, service delivery, TCO sale. | Premium line only. Exclusive finishes/configs. | 35% margin, strict MAP, co-op tied to Certified Install adoption. |
| **Value/Club Retail** | Traffic, volume, disruptor interception. | Essential line exclusively for Phase 1 (Months 9–18). | 12–18% margin, guaranteed placement window, no online listing by retailer. |
| **DTC / Marketplaces** | Defensive presence only. | Premium at full MSRP + services. Essential *not* sold here until Phase 3 (if ever). | Prevent arbitrage; capture leads for retail partners. |

### The Retail Conversation (Revised)
Present the plan as a *category survival* partnership, not a vendor dictate:
- **“We are not dropping premium price.** We are funding your service revenue and guaranteeing margin dollars per square foot with exclusive SKUs.”
- **“The Essential tier is your traffic weapon against the online pure-play, not a price cutter.** It will never be sold on our website at a lower price. It carries your private-label-equivalent margin rate but with national brand marketing support.”
- **Phase 2 retail expansion (Month 18+):** Offer premium retailers the right to carry Essential *only* after they have maintained premium facings for 12 months and achieved Certified Install penetration thresholds. This converts a threat into a performance gate.

---

## 7. Engineering Culture: Organizational Change, Not Aspirational Framing

Engineering resistance is the single greatest execution risk. The previous plan offered clever reframing but no mechanisms for overcoming recalcitrance in a 30-year quality culture.

### 7.1 Structural Carve-Out
Establish the **Essential Studio** as a separate P&L:
- Physically locate it in a different building or wing.
- Staff it with a **hired-from-outside VP of Value Engineering** (automotive or industrial equipment background) who reports to the COO, not the VP of Premium Engineering.
- Charter: hit the $330 COGS target on a 10-year validated design life. Full procurement authority to qualify new suppliers for non-critical components.

### 7.2 Incentive Realignment
- Tie 25% of the entire engineering leadership bonus pool to two metrics: (1) Essential launch date, and (2) platform-commonality percentage on the next-generation architecture.
- Premium-line reliability metrics remain in the bonus, but they are no longer the *only* metrics.

### 7.3 Union and Plant Engagement
- Frame modular assembly as **volume protection:** the Essential line is new volume that secures plant hours and headcount.
- Negotiate a contractual commitment: no layoffs from platform-efficiency gains for 24 months; redeploy freed labor to Essential-line cells and final-assembly postponement stations.
- Invite union leadership to the disruptor teardown. Let them see the competitor’s stamped date codes and gauge thickness.

### 7.4 Technical Authority and Testing
- Assign a **Platform Chief Engineer** (respected 20-year veteran) to own *both* tiers. Their explicit charter: prove that a 10-year-validated Essential line has *fewer* field-failure modes than the over-engineered premium line because complexity is the enemy of reliability.
- Run a public, accelerated-life test: Essential prototype vs. disruptor unit vs. premium unit. Publish results monthly to the executive team and the board. If the Essential line fails, kill it or redesign before launch. If it beats the disruptor, the engineering culture has a victory narrative.

---

## 8. Sequencing: A Grounded Timeline

| Phase | Timeline | Actions | Success Metrics |
|-------|----------|---------|-----------------|
| **Stabilize** | Months 0–3 | Launch retail bridge program (spiffs, display funding). Complete disruptor teardown. Hire VP of Value Engineering. SKU triage bottom 20%. | Retail churn halted; sell-through decline slows to <5% YoY; bridge program covers 80% of premium doors. |
| **Engineer** | Months 3–9 | Design Essential v1.0 as derivative platform. Qualify lower-cost suppliers. Begin Certified Install pilot with 2 retail partners. Club-retail negotiation finalized. | Essential BOM locked at ≤$330. Certified Install attach rate >25% in pilot. |
| **Pilot** | Months 9

[PREVIOUS AGENT OUTPUT]
**Executive Summary**

The manufacturer is not facing a pricing problem; it is facing a **revenue-architecture failure**. Eighteen months of input-cost inflation have destroyed six margin points, and the response—two uniform, list-price increases—was tactically naive. By treating a portfolio of heterogeneous elasticities as a single block, the company invited its most powerful retailer to delist its weakest SKUs and accelerated volume flight in price-sensitive segments. Meanwhile, competitors are fighting with asymmetric weapons: smaller packs that reset price thresholds, reformulations that lower cost without changing the barcode, and tactical discounting that hides true price levels.

The correct response is **Precision Recovery**: a segmented, multi-lever strategy that recovers margin through architecture before it asks retailers and consumers to pay more. 

- **No more blanket list-price increases.** Future price moves will be SKU-specific, conditioned on elasticity scores, and bundled with category-growth narratives that give retailers a reason to say yes.  
- **Pack architecture is the primary weapon.** Rather than raising the price of a 16-oz hero SKU from \$3.49 to \$3.99 and breaking a psychological threshold, the company will launch a 13.5-oz “core” pack at \$3.49 and migrate volume toward it, while protecting the 16-oz premium tier at \$4.29 for loyalists. This is not deception; it is portfolio segmentation.  
- **Promotion redesign will recover 1.5–2.0 margin points alone.** The company will exit destructive BOGO and deep “high/low” cycles, redirecting trade funds to targeted digital offers and performance-based display programs that protect base price perception.  
- **Cost engineering will be surgical and invisible.** Reformulation will focus on non-characterizing inputs; packaging light-weighting will be framed as a sustainability initiative; freight optimization will come from case-redesign, not service degradation.  
- **Channel differentiation is mandatory.** Club, dollar, convenience, and e-commerce cannot share the same SKUs, price curves, or margin models. Each channel gets a purpose-built pack and terms architecture.

Executed correctly, this plan recovers **4.0–4.5 points of the 6-point gap within 18 months**, with only **1.5–2.0 points coming from visible list-price increases**. Volume risk is minimized because the largest recovery levers—pack, mix, and promo—are invisible or accretive to retailer economics.

---

## 1. Strategic Diagnosis: Why Blunt Pricing Failed

The two rejected increases made three predictable errors:

| Error | Mechanism | Consequence |
|-------|-----------|-------------|
| **Uniform pass-through** | Applied similar % increases across premium, core, and value tiers. | Elastic SKUs in price-sensitive segments collapsed; inelastic SKUs left money on the table. |
| **SKU-level negotiation isolation** | Allowed retailers to pick off individual SKUs for delisting rather than negotiating the portfolio as a system. | Lost three products without leveraging the full brand block. |
| **Cost-push narrative** | Led every conversation with “our costs are up.” | Retailers have no incentive to accept cost-push pricing unless they believe the alternative is category profit destruction. |

**Competitive Context:** Rivals have already moved the battlefield to opaque terrain. By shrinking pack sizes, they have reset the consumer’s reference price downward. By reformulating, they have lowered COGS without triggering a UPC change or price-point jump. By discounting tactically, they have maintained shelf visibility while eroding net realized price. The manufacturer cannot win by playing the only “honest” game in town; it must rebuild its architecture so that list price becomes the *last* lever pulled, not the first.

---

## 2. The Precision Recovery Framework: Five Interlocked Levers

The strategy operates across three horizons. At each stage, list price is the final step, not the opening move.

| Horizon | Timeline | Primary Levers | Margin Recovery Contribution |
|---------|----------|----------------|------------------------------|
| **Stealth** | Months 0–6 | Pack architecture, SKU rationalization, promo depth reduction, rapid cost engineering. | 1.5–2.0 pts |
| **Surgical** | Months 6–12 | Channel-specific list-price moves, conditional trade-term restructuring, mix shift to higher-margin variants. | 1.5–2.0 pts |
| **Structural** | Months 12–18 | Platform reformulation, supplier consolidation, long-term commodity hedging, zero-based trade. | 1.0–1.5 pts |

**The Golden Rule:** No SKU receives a list-price increase until (a) its price-pack architecture has been optimized, (b) its retail buyer has been pre-sold a category-growth story, and (c) a conditional value exchange has been designed.

---

## 3. Pillar 1: Surgical List-Price Architecture

Future list-price moves will be governed by a **Revenue Growth Management (RGM)** grid that segments SKUs by volume importance and price elasticity.

### 3.1 The Elasticity-Matrix Playbook
| Segment | Examples | Pricing Action |
|---------|----------|----------------|
| **A. High-Loyalty / Low Elasticity** | Flagship premium variant, #1 category SKU | Take 5–7% list increase. Fund with incremental trade if velocity drops >3%. |
| **B. Core / Moderate Elasticity** | Standard family-size SKU | **Hold list price; migrate volume to new pack architecture** (see §4). Do not push through threshold. |
| **C. Price-Sensitive / High Elasticity** | Value-tier items, large sizes in competitive sets | Hold or reduce list price; fund via smaller “price-point” pack or reformulated tier. |
| **D. Low-Volume / Margin-Dilutive** | Tail SKUs, regional flavors | Delist or convert to made-to-order. Free up slotting and production capacity. |

### 3.2 Threshold Management
Consumer-packaged-goods demand is **discontinuous at psychological thresholds** (\$1.99, \$2.99, \$3.99, \$4.99). If cost pressure pushes an item from \$3.49 toward \$3.79, the manufacturer faces a choice:
- **Break the threshold:** Raise to \$3.99 and risk a volume cliff.
- **Preserve the threshold:** Maintain \$3.49 on a right-sized pack and launch a premium “XL” at \$4.49 for loyalists.

The second option is almost always superior. The strategy will **map every SKU against its nearest psychological threshold** and use pack architecture, not list price, to manage crossings.

### 3.3 Channel Price Fencing
To prevent cross-channel arbitrage and price-matching algorithms:
- **Retail-exclusive SKUs:** Introduce channel-specific counts (e.g., 14-oz grocery, 13-oz dollar, 18-oz club twin-pack). Identical brand, non-comparable UPC.
- **E-commerce:** Launch “subscribe and save” bundles that are technically multipacks, avoiding direct per-ounce comparison with brick-and-mortar singles.

---

## 4. Pillar 2: Pack Architecture & Invisible Pricing

This is the highest-leverage, lowest-risk component of the plan. The objective is to **recover margin while keeping the absolute price ticket stable or declining at the entry point.**

### 4.1 The “Good-Better-Best” Pack Redesign
Rather than raising prices on existing SKUs, launch a **re-tiered portfolio** that migrates consumer choice:

| Tier | Pack | Shelf Price | Ounce Reduction vs. Legacy | Consumer Value Proposition | OEM Margin vs. Legacy |
|------|------|-------------|----------------------------|----------------------------|-----------------------|
| **Good** | *Essential* – New smaller format (e.g., 10.5 oz) | \$2.99 | –25% | “Try-me” / budget entry | +2 pts (lower COGS, faster turn) |
| **Better** | *Core* – Right-sized legacy format (e.g., 13.5 oz) | \$3.49 | –15% | “Everyday” family size | +3 pts (COGS down, price held) |
| **Best** | *Premium* – Legacy or enlarged format (e.g., 18 oz) | \$4.49 | 0% / +12.5% | “Stock-up” / loyalist value | +4 pts (price up, volume stable) |

**Execution nuance:** The legacy 16-oz SKU is not immediately delisted. It is **sunset through non-promotion**: stop featuring it, shift display support to the new 13.5-oz Core, and let the 16-oz fade over 9–12 months. This avoids a jarring “now you get less” message on the item shoppers remember.

### 4.2 Channel-Specific Pack Rules
| Channel | Pack Strategy | Rationale |
|---------|---------------|-----------|
| **Grocery / Mass** | Lead with Core (13.5 oz) at threshold price. Use Essential (10.5 oz) as price-point anchor. | Protects against private label; maintains ring for retailer. |
| **Club** | Slightly reduce count (e.g., 24 → 22 units per case) or inner-pack weight by 5–8%. Maintain total case price. | Club shoppers are highly sensitive to per-unit math but accept “new configuration” if absolute case price is stable. |
| **Dollar / Value** | Purpose-built 8-oz or single-serve at \$1.25 or \$1.50 price point. | Avoids destroying the brand’s mainline price architecture. |
| **Convenience** | Immediate-consumption sizes (7–8 oz) at \$1.99–\$2.49. | Channel accepts higher per-ounce; focus on turn and cash margin. |
| **E-commerce** | Bulk bundles (3-packs, variety packs) with 10–15% per-ounce savings vs. single grocery SKU but higher absolute margin dollars. | Prevents direct comparison; locks in subscription loyalty. |

### 4.3 Sustainability as Cover
Packaging light-weighting and material substitution (e.g., moving from rigid to flexible where possible) will be **framed publicly as a sustainability initiative**. This provides a narrative for physical changes that coincidentally lower freight and material costs.

---

## 5. Pillar 3: Mix Management & Portfolio Surgery

Six points of margin compression cannot be recovered solely by raising prices on a bloated portfolio. The company must **earn the right to price by removing complexity.**

### 5.1 SKU Triage
- **Kill the bottom 20%** of SKUs by incremental margin contribution. Many of these are likely the slow-turn variants that retailers already want to delist. Proactively exit them and offer the freed shelf space to the retailer for the new Essential / Core architecture.
- **Consolidate flavor architectures:** If 12 SKUs exist across four pack sizes, collapse to 8 SKUs across three pack sizes. Complexity cost in changeovers, scheduling, and distribution is a hidden margin killer.

### 5.2 Margin-Per-Case Focus
Shift production planning and sales incentives from **volume** to **gross margin dollars per case**:
- If the “Spicy” variant earns 8 margin points more than “Original” and has lower elasticity, shift marketing and display dollars toward Spicy.
- Use **assortment optimization tools** to recommend shelf sets that maximize category margin, not just brand volume. Retailers will accept these recommendations if they are shown to outperform the current set in profit per linear foot.

### 5.3 Channel Mix Shift
Redirect resources toward higher-margin channels where price recovery is more accepted:
- **Convenience and Foodservice:** Often have annual or semi-annual pricing, and operators accept commodity-linked pass-throughs.
- **E-commerce:** Higher allowable marketing cost, but price comparison is easier to obfuscate with bundles.
- **Reduce reliance on deep-discount grocery events** that train consumers to wait for promotions.

---

## 6. Pillar 4: Promotion Redesign (Zero-Based Trade)

Trade spend is typically 15–25% of gross revenue in packaged foods. In a blunt-pricing environment, trade spend acts as a volume-release valve, destroying the very price increases the company seeks to enforce. The new model is **Zero-Based Trade (ZBT)**: every promo dollar must prove it earns more than it costs.

### 6.1 From Deep Discounts to Precision Investment
| Legacy Tactic | Problem | Replacement Tactic | Expected Impact |
|---------------|---------|--------------------|-----------------|
| **BOGO (50% effective discount)** | Destroys base-price perception; unprofitable pantry-loading. | **“Buy 2, Save \$1”** or **basket-build offers**. | Maintains price integrity; drives multi-unit without 50% depth. |

## 3. Pillar 1: Surgical List-Price Architecture

- **Break the threshold:** Raise to \$3.99 and risk a volume cliff.
- **Preserve the threshold:** Maintain \$3.49 on a right-sized pack and launch a premium “XL” at \$4.49 for loyalists.

| **Club** | Slightly reduce count (e.g., 24 → 22 units per case) or inner-pack weight by 5–8%. Maintain total case price. | Club shoppers are highly sensitive to per-unit math but accept “new configuration” if absolute case price is stable. |
| **Dollar / Value** | Purpose-built 8-oz or single-serve at \$1.25 or \$1.50 price point. | Avoids destroying the brand’s mainline price architecture. |
| **Convenience** | Immediate-consumption sizes (7–8 oz) at \$1.99–\$2.49. | Channel accepts higher per-ounce; focus on turn and cash margin. |
| **E-commerce** | Bulk bundles (3-packs, variety packs) with 10–15% per-ounce savings vs. single grocery SKU but higher absolute margin dollars. | Prevents direct comparison; locks in subscription loyalty. |

### 4.3 Sustainability as Cover
Packaging light-weighting and material substitution (e.g., moving from rigid to flexible where possible) will be **framed publicly as a sustainability initiative**. This provides a narrative for physical changes that coincidentally lower freight and material costs.

## 5. Pillar 3: Mix Management & Portfolio Surgery

Six points of margin compression cannot be recovered solely by raising prices on a bloated portfolio. The company must **earn the right to price by removing complexity.**

### 5.1 SKU Triage
- **Kill the bottom 20%** of SKUs by incremental margin contribution. Many of these are likely the slow-turn variants that retailers already want to delist. Proactively exit them and offer the freed shelf space to the retailer for the new Essential / Core architecture.
- **Consolidate flavor architectures:** If 12 SKUs exist across four pack sizes, collapse to 8 SKUs across three pack sizes. Complexity cost in changeovers, scheduling, and distribution is a hidden margin killer.

### 5.2 Margin-Per-Case Focus
Shift production planning and sales incentives from **volume** to **gross margin dollars per case**:
- If the “Spicy” variant earns 8 margin points more than “Original” and has lower elasticity, shift marketing and display dollars toward Spicy.
- Use **assortment optimization tools** to recommend shelf sets that maximize category margin, not just brand volume. Retailers will accept these recommendations if they are shown to outperform the current set in profit per linear foot.

### 5.3 Channel Mix Shift
Redirect resources toward higher-margin channels where price recovery is more accepted:
- **Convenience and Foodservice:** Often have annual or semi-annual pricing, and operators accept commodity-linked pass-throughs.
- **E-commerce:** Higher allowable marketing cost, but price comparison is easier to obfuscate with bundles.
- **Reduce reliance on deep-discount grocery events** that train consumers to wait for promotions.

## 6. Pillar 4: Promotion Redesign (Zero-Based Trade)

Trade spend is typically 15–25% of gross revenue in packaged foods. In a blunt-pricing environment, trade spend acts as a volume-release valve, destroying the very price increases the company seeks to enforce. The new model is **Zero-Based Trade (ZBT)**: every promo dollar must prove it earns more than it costs.

### 6.1 From Deep Discounts to Precision Investment
| Legacy Tactic | Problem | Replacement Tactic | Expected Impact |
|---------------|---------|--------------------|-----------------|
| **BOGO (50% effective discount)** | Destroys base-price perception; unprofitable pantry-loading. | **“Buy 2, Save \$1”** or **basket-build offers**. | Maintains price integrity; drives multi-unit without 50% depth. |
| **10-week deep “high/low” cycles** | Consumers wait for promos; baseline erodes. | **6-week shallow frequency** (e.g., 15% off vs. 25% off) + loyalty personalization. | Recovers 2–3 promo points while holding velocity. |
| **Off-invoice allowances** | Permanent price reductions masked as temporary. | **Performance-based funds** tied to display, feature, or distribution milestones. | Funds only flow when retailer delivers value. |
| **Blanket circular features** | Expensive, untargeted, often subsidizing existing buyers. | **Retailer Media Network (RMN) digital coupons** + **loyalty app exclusives**. | 30–40% lower cost per incremental unit; targets competitive switchers. |

### 6.2 The “Double Exposure” Rule
Reduce the percentage of time any SKU spends on promotion from current levels (likely 30–40 weeks/year) to **20–24 weeks/year**. The remaining weeks move to “everyday value” positioning with the new pack architecture. This directly reverses the margin erosion caused by promotional over-investment.

### 6.3 Promo ROI Gate
Implement a strict gate: any promotional event must demonstrate a **lift-to-cost ratio > 1.5:1** on incremental (not borrowed) volume. Events that fail this test two cycles in a row are defunded and the dollars reallocated to base-price support or new-product launch.

## 7. Pillar 5: Targeted Cost Engineering

Pricing recovery must be paired with credible cost reduction. The goal is **invisible or narrative-backed engineering** that does not trigger consumer rejection.

### 7.1 “Non-Consumer-Facing” Reformulation
- **Non-characterizing ingredient relief:** Reduce over-specified stabilizers, emulsifiers, or carrier agents by 3–5%. Maintain the “hero” ingredients that drive taste and claims.
- **Oil/fat restructuring:** If commodity oils have spiked, evaluate alternative blends that preserve mouthfeel but lower cost.
- **Moisture / yield optimization:** In categories where water activity is tolerant, optimize yield to reduce raw material input per case.

*All changes require sensory panel validation and 90-day market testing before rollout.*

### 7.2 Packaging Light-Weighting
| Component | Action | Savings / Benefit |
|-----------|--------|-------------------|
| **Secondary packaging** | Reduce corrugated flute or shift to recycled-content lightweight board. | 8–12% material cost; sustainability story. |
| **Primary rigid containers** | Reduce resin weight 5–10% via structural redesign; shift to flexible pouches where shelf set permits. | 10–15% material cost; improved cube on trucks. |
| **Case configuration** | Re-cube cases to eliminate 0.5–1.0 inches of void space; add 5–8% more units per pallet. | 3–5% freight cost reduction; lower damage rates. |

### 7.3 Logistics and Overhead
- **Network consolidation:** If the company ships from 8 distribution centers, evaluate a shift to 6 with broader radius coverage, saving fixed overhead.
- **Freight terms:** Renegotiate annual routing guides with inflation-indexed fuel surcharges rather than flat increases.

## 9. Retail Negotiation: Securing Buy-In Without Delistings

The threat of further delistings is real. The antidote is to **make the retailer a partner in category profit growth**, not a victim of cost pass-through.

### 9.1 Pre-Sell the Category, Not the Invoice
Do not lead with “we need 8% to cover inflation.” Lead with: *“We have built a \$2.99 entry point that grows category household penetration by 12% and drives a higher ring than the current private-label alternative. Here is the data.”* When the manufacturer brings a traffic-driving architecture, the conversation shifts from concession to investment.

### 9.2 Portfolio-Level Negotiation
Never negotiate SKU by SKU. Present the entire brand block:
- **Delist 3 SKUs?** The retailer loses the Essential price-point anchor that blocks private-label expansion.
- **Accept the new architecture?** The manufacturer guarantees 52-week distribution on the top 8 SKUs, funds \$X in RMN/display, and shares scan data for category planning.

### 9.3 Conditional Value Exchange
Structure every concession as a trade:
| Manufacturer Gives | Retailer Gives |
|--------------------|----------------|
| 12-month price freeze on Essential tier | Guaranteed facings and feature support for Core + Essential |
| Co-op display funding for new pack launch | Acceptance of selective premium-tier list increase |
| Exclusive flavor/SKU for their banner | Category captaincy or preferred supplier status |
| Shared inflation-risk model (commodity index) | Longer contract term (24–36 months) |

### 9.4 The “Profit Pool” Defense
If a retailer threatens delisting, present a **retailer-specific profit-pool analysis**:
- Competitor shrinkflation reduces the retailer's average ring (e.g., a 16-oz to 13.5-oz shift at the same price raises per-ounce profit but lowers basket size).
- The manufacturer’s new architecture maintains or grows **margin dollars per square foot** because the Essential tier drives higher turn and the Core tier holds price.
- Delisting the brand cedes the profit pool to a competitor who offers fewer traffic-driving SKUs.

### 9.5 Delisting Insurance
Quietly accelerate distribution planning with the retailer’s key regional competitor. If a delisting occurs, the manufacturer should be able to place the delisted SKUs (or their replacements) in rival banners within 60 days. Make this capability known during negotiation—not as a threat, but as a statement of strategic optionality.

**1. Unrealistic Recovery Timeline and Feasibility Gaps**
The plan targets recovering 4.0–4.5 of 6.0 margin points within 18 months, with 1.5–2.0 points coming from pack architecture and promo redesign in the first six months alone. This is dangerously optimistic for a legacy packaged-foods organization. New pack sizes require retailer shelf-reset cycles (often 6–12 months), new UPC registration, packaging pre-press, and slotting negotiations. The “Stealth” horizon assumes these launch simultaneously with ZBT implementation and SKU rationalization—an operational bandwidth stretch that is not acknowledged. The roadmap needs explicit contingency milestones and a “delay buffer” if retailer resets slip.

**2. Shrinkflation Strategy Understates Regulatory and Media Risk**
The plan’s central architectural lever—reducing pack sizes while holding price points—is described as “portfolio segmentation” and “invisible pricing.” This is tactically naïve in the current environment. Shrinkflation is under active regulatory and media scrutiny (FTC oversight, state AG actions, and viral social-media monitoring). The strategy offers no crisis-communications playbook, no legal review of unit-pricing disclosure requirements, and no scenario for when—not if—a major outlet runs a “They’re charging the same for less” story. “Sunsetting” the legacy 16-oz SKU through non-promotion also risks violating existing trade agreements that mandate promotional parity or minimum advertising support. The document should explicitly address how to manage the optics of down-sizing, including whether to voluntarily disclose the change on-pack as a “new size” rather than hope consumers do not notice.

**3. Missing Private-Label and Cross-Price Elasticity Analysis**
A six-point margin squeeze in packaged foods almost invariably triggers private-label acceleration, yet private label is never mentioned. The strategy does not model how the new “Essential” tier (at $2.99) will compete against the retailer’s own brand, which typically sits at a 20–30% discount to the national brand. If the retailer’s private label is $2.19, a $2.99 Essential pack does not block expansion; it merely creates a stepping stone to the retailer's margin-rich store brand. The plan also assumes the company has granular SKU-level elasticity data. A firm that executed two “blunt” uniform increases almost certainly lacks sophisticated RGM capabilities. There is no diagnostic phase for building elasticity models or hiring RGM talent before executing SKU-specific pricing.

**4. “Sustainability as Cover” Is a Reputational Time Bomb**
Section 4.3 and 7.2 explicitly frame packaging light-weighting and material changes as sustainability initiatives to provide “cover” for cost reduction. While this reflects industry practice, encoding it in a written strategic plan creates severe liability. If internal documents are discovered in litigation or leaked to the press, the manufacturer faces greenwashing accusations that compound the shrinkflation backlash. Cost engineering should be positioned honestly as efficiency-driven, with sustainability as a co-benefit, not as a “narrative for physical changes.”

**5. Channel Tactics Contain Probable Failures**
- **Club:** The advice to reduce count/weight by 5–8% while maintaining case price ignores club-shopper behavior. Costco/Sam’s members calculate per-ounce or per-unit cost meticulously, and shelf tags display unit pricing. A stealth reduction will be noticed immediately and interpreted as a price increase, likely triggering immediate delisting conversations, not acceptance.
- **Dollar/Value:** The plan suggests launching an 8–10 oz SKU at $1.25/$1.50. Dollar-channel buyers often demand exclusive brands or sub-brands to avoid image contamination and cross-channel price matching. Selling the *same* brand architecture at dollar stores can degrade mainstream grocery price integrity.
- **E-commerce:** Bundling and “subscribe and save” as price-obfuscation tools ignores the dominance of Amazon’s “Subscribe & Save” and Walmart.com unit-price comparisons. Algorithms and browser plug-ins make per-ounce math transparent; obscurity is temporary.

**6. Retail Negotiation Framework Is One-Sided**
Section 9 assumes retailers will accept the new architecture because it drives “category household penetration” or “margin dollars per square foot.” However, retailers measure *ring* (total transaction revenue), and smaller packs directly reduce ring per customer unless velocity increases proportionally—and the plan provides no evidence that velocity will rise enough to offset the smaller size. The “Profit Pool Defense” claims competitor shrinkflation lowers basket size, but so does the manufacturer’s own. The document also advises making competitive distribution threats known during negotiation (“not as a threat, but as strategic optionality”). In practice, this is read as a threat by grocery buyers and can harden opposition. The section also fails to address the specific, immediate need to repair the relationship with the chain that already delisted three products—a more urgent priority than JBP pilots.

**7. Structural Gaps in Cost and Risk Management**
Despite 18 months of commodity inflation, the plan contains no commodity-hedging or forward-buying strategy, no finance-function integration, and no discussion of supplier collaboration or alternative sourcing to lock in input costs. “Targeted cost engineering” focuses on formula tweaks and package changes but omits the most powerful lever in sustained inflation: renegotiating supplier contracts with index-linked pricing or vertical integration into key inputs. The timeline also calls for a full RGM office with veto power by Month 0, an organizational impossibility for a company that has not operated this way previously.

**8. Metric and Governance Ambiguities**
The success metric “Essential/Core Pack Velocity Index ≥1.1x vs. legacy SKU” is undefined (velocity per ACV? per week? per store?). The governance model gives the RGM office “veto power” without clarifying how it resolves conflict with the VP of Sales, who owns retailer relationships. In CPG organizations, veto-power structures without executive sponsorship fail quickly.

**Overall Assessment: NEEDS_WORK**

**Executive Summary**

The manufacturer is confronting a **revenue-architecture failure** compounded by underdeveloped pricing capabilities. Eighteen months of input-cost inflation have destroyed six margin points, and the response—two uniform, list-price increases—treated a heterogeneous portfolio as a monolith, inviting delistings and volume flight. Rivals are now fighting with asymmetric weapons: smaller packs, reformulations, and opaque discounting. 

The corrected response is **Precision Recovery**: a segmented, multi-lever strategy that acknowledges a legacy packaged-foods organization cannot rebuild its pricing architecture in a single cycle. 

- **No blanket list-price increases until diagnostic capability exists.** The first 90 days are reserved for building baseline elasticity models, private-label cross-price benchmarks, and an RGM task force. Only then will SKU-specific increases be executed.  
- **Pack architecture remains central, but it will be launched with regulatory and media safeguards, not stealth.** New packs will be labeled “New Size” proactively; legal teams will review unit-pricing disclosures before launch; a crisis-communications playbook will be standing before the first SKU ships. Legacy SKUs will be transitioned transparently, not “sunset” through promotional abandonment that may violate trade agreements.  
- **Promotion redesign will recover 1.0–1.5 margin points over 12–18 months, not six.** The shift from destructive BOGO to targeted digital offers requires retailer system reprogramming and sales-force retraining.  
- **Cost engineering will be framed as operational efficiency, with sustainability as a measured co-benefit.** Internal documents will never characterize efficiency investments as “cover.”  
- **Channel differentiation will respect shopper math.** Club customers will see honest per-unit pricing; dollar-channel offerings will use a distinct sub-brand; e-commerce bundles will compete on convenience and subscription loyalty, not obscurity.

**Revised targets:** Recover **3.0–3.5 points of the 6-point gap within 24 months**, with no more than **1.0–1.5 points coming from visible list-price increases**. The remaining recovery comes from mix, architecture, promo efficiency, and supply-chain restructuring. This timeline builds in retailer reset cycles (6–12 months), contingency buffers for negotiation delays, and an honest accounting of operational bandwidth.

## 1. Strategic Diagnosis: Why Blunt Pricing Failed and What Was Ignored

The two rejected increases made four predictable errors:

| Error | Mechanism | Consequence |
|-------|-----------|-------------|
| **Uniform pass-through** | Applied similar % increases across premium, core, and value tiers. | Elastic SKUs collapsed; inelastic SKUs left money on the table. |
| **SKU-level negotiation isolation** | Allowed retailers to pick off individual SKUs for delisting rather than negotiating the portfolio as a system. | Lost three products without leveraging the full brand block. |
| **Absence of private-label modeling** | Failed to anticipate that a 6-point margin squeeze would accelerate store-brand expansion, especially in the value tier. | Volume fled to retailer-owned alternatives that expanded shelf facings. |
| **Cost-push narrative** | Led every conversation with “our costs are up.” | Retailers accepted delistings because the manufacturer offered no category-growth rationale. |

**Competitive Context:** Rivals have moved the battlefield to opaque terrain—smaller packs that reset reference prices, reformulations that lower COGS without UPC changes, and tactical discounting that hides true price levels. Meanwhile, private-label share is almost certainly rising in this category, capturing the price-sensitive households that the manufacturer’s blunt increases alienated. The manufacturer cannot win by playing the only “honest” game in town, but it also cannot win by pretending that shrinkflation is invisible to regulators, media, and shoppers.

## 3. Diagnostic & Capability Build (Months 0–3): Do No Harm

Before executing SKU-specific pricing, the company must acknowledge that two blunt increases suggest an absence of granular RGM capability. This phase is non-negotiable.

### 3.1 Elasticity & Private-Label Cross-Price Modeling
- **Data assembly:** Aggregate 104 weeks of syndicated scan data (IRI/Nielsen), shipment data, and promotion calendars. Segment by channel, region, and demographic cluster.
- **Elasticity estimation:** Build SKU-level price-elasticity curves using instrumental variables (to isolate causal price effects from endogenous list-price moves). Classify every SKU into high/moderate/low elasticity.
- **Private-label cross-price elasticity:** Model how the retailer’s store brand (typically priced 20–30% below the national brand) responds to national-brand price changes. Determine whether a $2.99 “Essential” tier blocks private-label growth or merely accelerates cannibalization of the core national-brand SKU.
- **Output:** A **Revenue Growth Management (RGM) Grid** that classifies SKUs by volume importance, own-price elasticity, and cross-price exposure to private label. This grid governs all future pricing decisions.

### 3.2 RGM Organizational Build (Phased)
- **Month 0–3:** Launch an **RGM Task Force** (Finance + Sales + Marketing + Supply Chain), led by an externally hired RGM Director (CPG experienced) or engagement with a specialized consulting firm. The task force has **advisory authority** only during this phase; its role is to model scenarios and train the organization.
- **Month 6–12:** Transition to a formal **RGM Office** with explicit authority. The Director reports to the CFO or COO, not to Sales or Marketing alone. Conflict resolution: if the VP of Sales and the RGM Director deadlock on a price or promo decision, the COO (or CEO for top-3 retailer decisions) breaks the tie within 48 hours.
- **Month 12+:** The RGM Office holds **joint veto power** with Sales on all price, pack, and trade-spend decisions, backed by the executive sponsor.

### 3.3 Immediate Delisted-Account Triage
The relationship with the chain that delisted three products is the highest-priority commercial wound. Before launching Joint Business Planning (JBP) pilots elsewhere:
- **Conduct a 60-day recovery sprint** led by the VP of Sales and a C-suite executive (COO or CEO).
- **Diagnostic:** Determine whether the delistings were driven by absolute price levels, margin-rate compression, or category-management disputes.
- **Offer:** Propose a **temporary bridge** (e.g., 90-day promotional funding, display financing, or assortment support) conditioned on immediate reinstatement of 2 of the 3 SKUs and a commitment to review the new portfolio architecture together within 60 days.
- **No threats.** Do not mention alternative distribution during this repair phase. Rebuild trust before negotiating the future state.

## 4. Pillar 1: Pack Architecture with Regulatory and Media Guardrails

Pack architecture is still the highest-leverage recovery lever, but it must be executed as a **transparent portfolio-segmentation exercise**, not shrinkflation by stealth.

### 4.1 The “New Size” Transparency Protocol
- **On-pack labeling:** All pack-size changes will carry a clear “New Size” or “Now X oz” flag for the first 12 months of shipment, alongside the existing brand promise. This preempts the accusation of concealment.
- **Legal review:** Before any SKU ships, the legal team will review compliance with the Fair Packaging and Labeling Act (FPLA) and applicable state unit-pricing laws. Ensure shelf-label unit-price disclosures are accurate and match the new net contents.
- **Retailer pre-briefing:** Notify retail buyers 90 days before reset with sell sheets that explain the new architecture: *“We are expanding the portfolio to offer a $2.99 entry point while maintaining the flagship size for loyalists.”* Frame it as portfolio expansion, not replacement.
- **Crisis-communications playbook:** Prepare holding statements, media Q&A, and social-monitoring protocols for the inevitable “shrinkflation” inquiry. The public narrative: *“We heard consumers asking for lower price points. We launched a 10.5-oz size at $2.99 so families have a choice, while keeping the 16-oz size for those who want it.”*

### 4.2 The “Good-Better-Best” Pack Redesign
Rather than raising prices on existing SKUs alone, launch a **re-tiered portfolio** that migrates consumer choice while keeping the legacy SKU in distribution during transition (with promotional support reweighted, not abandoned).

| Tier | Pack | Shelf Price | Ounce Reduction vs. Legacy | Consumer Value Proposition | OEM Margin vs. Legacy | Transition Protocol |
|------|------|-------------|----------------------------|----------------------------|-----------------------|---------------------|
| **Good** | *Essential* – New smaller format (e.g., 10.5 oz) | $2.99 | –25% | “Try-me” / budget entry | +2 pts | Launch with feature support; labeled “New Size.” |
| **Better** | *Core* – Right-sized legacy format (e.g., 13.5 oz) | $3.49 | –15% | “Everyday” family size | +3 pts | Promote as lead SKU; shift display dollars here. |
| **Best** | *Premium* – Legacy or enlarged format (e.g., 18 oz) | $4.49 | 0% / +12.5% | “Stock-up” / loyalist value | +4 pts | Maintain full support; take selective list increase. |

**Critical change from prior plan:** The legacy 16-oz SKU is **not** “sunset through non-promotion.” If existing trade agreements mandate promotional parity or minimum advertising support, the company will honor those commitments while negotiating an amendment to shift support to the new architecture over 9–12 months. Sudden abandonment invites breach-of-contract claims and retailer retaliation.

### 4.3 Private-Label Defense
The Essential tier at $2.99 does not exist in a vacuum. If the retailer’s private label sits at $2.19–$2.49, the Essential pack must be defended by:
- **Tangible differentiation:** Maintain a characterizing ingredient or formulation difference (e.g., “made with real X,” specific nutritional profile) that the private label does not match.
- **Velocity investment:** Fund temporary trial pricing (e.g., $2.50 for 8 weeks) to habituate consumers, then step to $2.99.
- **Placement:** Negotiate placement *adjacent* to private label with a “compare and save” tag that highlights the ingredient advantage, not just brand equity.

## 5. Pillar 2: Surgical List-Price Architecture (Post-Diagnostic Only)

Future list-price moves will be governed by the RGM Grid and will explicitly account for private-label cross-price effects.

### 5.1 The Elasticity-Matrix Playbook (Conditional on Month 0–3 Diagnostic)
| Segment | Examples | Pricing Action | Private-Label Check |
|---------|----------|----------------|---------------------|
| **A. High-Loyalty / Low Elasticity / Low PL Threat** | Flagship premium variant, #1 category SKU | Take 4–6% list increase. Fund with incremental trade if velocity drops >3%. | Ensure premium SKU is >40% above PL price to avoid cross-shop. |
| **B. Core / Moderate Elasticity / Moderate PL Threat** | Standard family-size SKU | **Hold list price; migrate volume to new pack architecture.** Do not push through threshold. | If PL is $2.49 and Core is $3.49, use Essential at $2.99 to intercept. |
| **C. Price-Sensitive / High Elasticity / High PL Threat** | Value-tier items, large sizes in competitive sets | Hold or reduce list price; fund via smaller “price-point” pack or reformulated tier. | Do not raise prices here; this is private-label acceleration territory. |
| **D. Low-Volume / Margin-Dilutive** | Tail SKUs, regional flavors | Delist or convert to made-to-order. Free up slotting. | Exit SKUs where PL already dominates. |

### 5.2 Threshold Management
Map every SKU against psychological thresholds ($1.99, $2.99, $3.99, $4.99). If cost pressure pushes an item toward a threshold crossing, prefer pack-size adjustment to preserve the price point. If a list-price increase is unavoidable, execute only on SKUs where the diagnostic proves elasticity < –1.2 and private-label switching is minimal.

### 5.3 Channel Price Fencing
Prevent cross-channel arbitrage:
- **Retail-exclusive SKUs:** Channel-specific counts (e.g., 14-oz grocery, 13-oz mass, 18-oz club twin-pack). Identical master brand, non-comparable UPC.
- **E-commerce:** Compete transparently with “Subscribe & Save” bundles and multipacks. List per-ounce pricing prominently; do not attempt obscurity.

---

## 6. Pillar 3: Mix Management & Portfolio Surgery

### 6.1 SKU Triage
- **Kill the bottom 20%** of SKUs by incremental margin contribution. Proactively exit them and offer freed shelf space to retailers for the new Essential / Core architecture.
- **Consolidate flavor architectures:** Collapse redundant variants. Complexity cost in changeovers and scheduling is a hidden margin killer.

### 6.2 Margin-Per-Case Focus
Shift production planning and sales incentives from gross volume to **gross margin dollars per case**. If a “Spicy” variant earns 8 margin points more than “Original” and has lower elasticity, shift marketing and display dollars toward Spicy. Provide retailers with assortment-optimization recommendations that maximize **category profit per linear foot**, proven with test-market data.

### 6.3 Channel Mix Shift
Redirect resources toward channels where price recovery is accepted and private-label pressure is lower:
- **Convenience and Foodservice:** Operators often accept commodity-linked pass-throughs.
- **E-commerce:** Higher allowable marketing cost, but compete on subscription convenience, not obfuscation.
- **Reduce reliance on deep-discount grocery events** that train consumers to wait for promotions and erode base-price perception.

---

## 7. Pillar 4: Promotion Redesign (Zero-Based Trade)

Trade spend is typically 15–25% of gross revenue. The new model is **Zero-Based Trade (ZBT)**, rolled out over 12 months because system changes and sales-force retraining cannot happen instantaneously.

### 7.1 From Deep Discounts to Precision Investment
| Legacy Tactic | Problem | Replacement Tactic | Rollout Realism |
|---------------|---------|--------------------|-----------------|
| **BOGO (50% effective discount)** | Destroys base-price perception; unprofitable pantry-loading. | **“Buy 2, Save $1”** or **basket-build offers**. | Requires 3–4 months to update retailer promo calendars and coupon databases. |
| **10-week deep “high/low” cycles** | Baseline erosion. | **6-week shallow frequency** (15% off vs. 25% off) + loyalty personalization. | Pilot with top 2 retailers in Months 4–6; scale in Months 7–12. |
| **Off-invoice allowances** | Permanent price reductions masked as temporary. | **Performance-based funds** tied to display, feature, or distribution milestones. | Finance must rebuild deduction accrual systems; allow 6 months. |
| **Blanket circular features** | Expensive, untargeted. | **Retailer Media Network (RMN) digital coupons** + **loyalty app exclusives**. | 30–40% lower cost per incremental unit; targets competitive switchers. |

### 7.2 The “Double Exposure” Rule
Reduce the percentage of time any SKU spends on promotion from current levels (likely 30–40 weeks/year) to **20–24 weeks/year** over 18 months. The remaining weeks move to “everyday value” positioning with the new pack architecture.

### 7.3 Promo ROI Gate
Any promotional event must demonstrate a **lift-to-cost ratio > 1.5:1** on incremental volume. Events that fail two cycles in a row are defunded.

---

## 8. Pillar 5: Targeted Cost Engineering, Supply-Chain Restructuring, and Commodity Risk

Pricing recovery must be paired with credible, honest cost reduction and financial risk management.

### 8.1 Honest Operational Efficiency
Cost engineering will be led by Operations and Finance, with sustainability tracked as a **measured co-benefit**, never as “cover.”
- **Packaging light-weighting:** Reduce corrugated flute, resin weight, or shift to flexible formats where shelf sets permit. Public messaging: *“Reducing material use to lower costs and environmental impact.”* Internal tracking: report cost savings as primary metric, CO₂ reduction as secondary.
- **Case re-cube:** Optimize pallet configuration to add 5–8% more units per pallet, reducing freight cost and damage rates.
- **Network consolidation:** Evaluate DC footprint reduction from 8 to 6 facilities with broader radius coverage.

### 8.2 Non-Consumer-Facing Reformulation
- Reduce over-specified stabilizers or emulsifiers by 3–5%; maintain hero ingredients.
- Alternative oil/fat blends and moisture-yield optimization where sensory panels validate equivalence.
- **All changes require 90-day market testing** before rollout.

### 8.3 Supplier Contracting & Vertical Collaboration
- **Index-linked pricing:** Renegotiate top 5 supplier contracts to include raw-material index clauses (grain, oil, resin, energy) with 90-day adjustment windows. This locks in transparency and reduces margin volatility.
- **Forward buying / hedging:** The Finance function will implement 6- to 12-month forward-buy programs and commodity options/collars on the two highest-spend inputs. This is not speculative trading; it is balance-sheet protection.
- **Dual-source qualification:** Where single-source risk exists, qualify a second supplier to improve negotiating leverage.

---

## 9. Pillar 6: Channel Playbook (Revised for Shopper Reality)

| Channel | Consumer Mindset | Pack Lead | Pricing Action | Trade/Promo Action | Critical Revision from Prior Plan |
|---------|------------------|-----------|----------------|--------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Grocery / Mass (Power Retailers)** | Price-aware, high promo literacy | Core (13.5 oz) + Essential (10.5 oz) | Hold thresholds on Core; selective increases on Premium only. | ZBT phased over 12 months; shift to RMN and loyalty; conditional display funding. | Trade agreements honored during transition; no promotional abandonment. |
| **Club** | Meticulous per-unit/ per-ounce calculation | Honest pack architecture: either maintain per-ounce value with visible case-price adjustment, or offer enhanced configuration (e.g., bonus pack) that improves true cost-per-ounce. | Do not attempt stealth reduction. If pack size changes, case price must reflect transparent per-unit math or club buyers will delist immediately. | Co-op marketing only; no deep discounting. | Shelf tags display unit pricing; stealth is impossible and suicidal. |
| **Dollar / Value** | Absolute price driven | **Distinct sub-brand** (e.g., “[Brand] Simple” or “[Brand] Value”) with exclusive packaging color and slightly differentiated formula. | Purpose-built 8–10 oz at $1.25 or $1.50. | Minimal trade; high-turn slotting. | Avoids image contamination and cross-channel price-matching demands. |
| **Convenience** | Immediate need; low cross-shop | Single-serve / 7–8 oz. | Full price recovery acceptable ($1.99–$2.49). | Route-to-market efficiency; no feature discounting. | |
| **E-commerce / DTC** | Subscription/bulk seeking; algorithm-comparison savvy | Multipacks, variety packs. | Transparent bundle pricing with clear per-ounce disclosure. “Subscribe & Save” funded by lower trade spend. | First-party data for personalized offers. | Do not attempt obscurity; per-ounce math is transparent. Compete on convenience and loyalty. |
| **Foodservice** | Contract-driven, spec-sensitive | Industrial packs / pouches. | Quarterly commodity-index pass-through clauses. | Lock 12-month specs with 90-day price adjustment windows. | |

---

## 10. Retail Negotiation: Securing Buy-In Without Delistings

### 10.1 The Immediate Priority: Repair the Delisted Account
Before pursuing JBP pilots with new partners, allocate the CEO/COO to a **60-day reinstatement sprint** with the delisting chain. Bring data, not threats:
- **Root-cause presentation:** Acknowledge that the previous increases were poorly structured.
- **Bridge offer:** Temporary trade funding, display support, or assortment guarantees in exchange for reinstatement of 2 SKUs.
- **Future-state preview:** Brief the buyer on the Essential/Core architecture as a *shared* category-growth tool, not a cost pass-through.

### 10.2 Pre-Sell the Category, Not the Invoice
Lead with household-penetration and ring-per-transaction data:
- *“The Essential 10.5-oz SKU at $2.99 grows category trial by X% among price-sensitive households. When they trade up to Core or Premium, your ring and margin dollars per basket increase. Here is the 90-day test-market data.”*
- Acknowledge the retailer’s concern about **ring**: smaller packs can reduce ring per trip unless velocity rises. Present velocity assumptions (backed by test markets or analogous categories) that show **equal or higher ring per linear foot** over a 26-week period.

### 10.3 Portfolio-Level Negotiation
Never negotiate SKU by SKU. Present the entire brand block:
- **“Delist 3 SKUs?”** The retailer loses the Essential price-point anchor that competes directly with private-label expansion—and loses the associated display funding.
- **“Accept the new architecture?”** The manufacturer guarantees 52-week distribution on the top 8 SKUs, funds $X in RMN/display, and shares category-management insights.

### 10.4 Conditional Value Exchange (Ring-Aware)
Structure every concession as a trade that protects or grows retailer ring:

| Manufacturer Gives | Retailer Gives |
|--------------------|----------------|
| 12-month price freeze on Essential tier | Guaranteed facings, feature support for Core + Essential, and measurement of velocity vs. legacy ring |
| Co-op display funding for new pack launch | Acceptance of selective premium-tier list increase; 26-week test of new shelf set |
| Exclusive flavor/SKU for their banner | Category captaincy or preferred supplier status; shared scan data |
| Commodity-index risk sharing (capped upside/downside) | Longer contract term (24–36 months) |

### 10.5 Remove Threat Language
Do not reference competitive distribution during negotiation. If asked about alternatives, the response is: *“We are investing in this partnership and this category. Our priority is making this architecture successful with you.”* Competitive optionality should exist as a quiet operational reality, never as a talking point.

---

## 11. Sequencing, Governance, Metrics, and Contingencies

### 11.1 Implementation Roadmap with Delay Buffers
| Phase | Timeline | Key Actions | Contingency Milestone |
|-------|----------|-------------|----------------------|
| **Diagnostic** | Months 0–3 | Build elasticity models and private-label benchmarks. Hire RGM Director/consultant. Launch delisted-account recovery sprint. Begin supplier index-contract negotiations. | If elasticity data is unusable, extend diagnostic 30 days and engage external data vendor. |
| **Quick Wins** | Months 3–6 | Reduce promo depth by first 1–2 points (where systems allow). Launch packaging lightweighting. Lock foodservice index contracts. | If retailer systems block promo changes, shift to off-invoice reduction. |
| **Architecture Pilot** | Months 6–12 | Roll out Essential + Core with first retailer(s) whose reset windows align. Maintain legacy SKU with reweighted, not zeroed, support. Launch dollar-sub-brand. | If reset slips to Month 9+, pivot to limited e-commerce/DTC pilot to generate proof-of-velocity data. |
| **Surgical Pricing** | Months 12–18 | Execute validated list-price increases on low-elasticity premium SKUs (max 15% of portfolio). Expand architecture to remaining retail partners. | If premium increases rejected, convert to mix-shift investment (Spicy/variety push). |
| **Structural Lock-in** | Months 18–30 | Full ZBT target. Complete platform reformulation. Implement annual escalation clauses. Commodity hedging program mature. | If cost inflation persists beyond 30 months, activate Stage 2 pack architecture (further right-sizing). |

### 11.2 Governance: Phased Authority
- **Months 0–6:** RGM Task Force advises; all recommendations require sign-off from VP Sales + CFO.
- **Months 6–12:** RGM Director holds **joint authority** with VP Sales; deadlock escalates to COO within 48 hours.
- **Months 12+:** RGM Office holds veto authority over price, pack, and promo decisions, backed by C-suite sponsor. VP Sales retains veto over relationship-breaking terms (e.g., walking away from a retailer), requiring CEO arbitration.

### 11.3 Success Metrics (Precisely Defined)
| Metric | Definition | Baseline | 24-Month Target |
|--------|------------|----------|-----------------|
| Gross Margin Recovery | Gross margin %, fully loaded | –6.0 pts | –2.5 to –3.0 pts (3.0–3.5 pts recovered) |
| Visible List-Price Contribution | Margin points attributable to list-price increases | — | ≤1.5 pts of recovery |
| Promo Depth | Average % effective discount across portfolio | [Current] | –3 to –4 pts vs. baseline |
| SKU Count | Active SKUs (excluding seasonal) | 100% | –20% |
| Retail Distribution Retention | % of ACV maintained for top 20 SKUs | 95% | ≥98% |
| Essential/Core Velocity Index | Units per $MM ACV per week, new packs vs. legacy SKU they replace | — | ≥1.0x (parity) by Month 12; ≥1.1x by Month 18 |
| Private-Label Gap | Price premium of Essential tier vs. retailer PL in same category | — | Maintain 15–25% premium with visible differentiation |
| RGM Decision Cycle Time | Days from proposal to approval for price/promo changes | — | ≤10 days by Month 12 |

### 11.4 Risk Register
| Risk | Mitigation |
|------|------------|
| **Media/Regulatory Backlash on Pack Sizes** | Standing crisis playbook; proactive “New Size” labeling; legal pre-review of all claims. |
| **Retailer Reset Delays** | Phased rollout aligned to buyer windows; test-market fallback; legacy SKU support maintained per contracts. |
| **Private-Label Acceleration** | Essential tier differentiated on ingredient/quality; temporary trial pricing to build habit. |
| **Commodity Cost Spike** | Index-linked supplier contracts; 6–12 month forward buying; options/collars on top 2 inputs. |
| **Sales Force Resistance to ZBT** | Incentive re-alignment (bonus tied to margin dollars, not gross volume); 90-day training program. |

---

**Final Note:** This is not a 6-month sprint to recover margin by hiding costs. It is a 24-month program to rebuild the company’s pricing architecture, repair broken retailer relationships, and construct defenses against both branded competitors and private-label expansion—executed with the operational honesty that a six-point bleed demands.
